title: An item id is used as a file path without validation

sections.heading: Why
sections.body:
`ids.allocate` checks that an id is unique and nothing else. The id then becomes a
filename: `store.slice_path` joins it onto `.slicer/slices/`, and `promote` writes there.
Nothing between the two rejects a separator or a parent reference.

    $ slicer add "escapee" --id '../../../pwned'
    $ slicer promote '../../../pwned'
    promoted ../../../pwned -> .../proj/.slicer/slices/../../../pwned.json

That file lands three levels above the tracking directory — outside the project. A
gentler one, `--id 'S/1'`, silently creates `.slicer/slices/S/1.json`, a subdirectory the
loader does not scan, so the slice becomes invisible while the index still claims it
exists. `slicer check` passes on both.

**This is not only reachable through `--id`.** `legacy._parse_row` returns whatever sits
in the first table cell as the item id, with no character rule:

    >>> legacy._parse_row('| [../evil](../evil.md) | t | M | x | f | done |', ...).item_id
    '../evil'

So `slicer migrate` pointed at a markdown tree someone else wrote can write outside the
project. The docs actively encourage migrating an existing tree, which makes that a
realistic path rather than a theoretical one.

Filed at M rather than S because the fix has to cover three entry points and decide what
happens to a project that already contains a bad id.

sections.heading: Files
sections.body:
- `src/slicer/ids.py` — `allocate`, and a character rule to share
- `src/slicer/store.py` — `slice_path`, as the last line of defence
- `src/slicer/migrator.py` — ids adopted from a legacy tree
- `src/slicer/verify.py` — report an id already stored that breaks the rule

sections.heading: Failing tests
sections.body:
1. `Add_IdWithASeparator_IsRefused`, for `/` and `\` and `..`.
2. `Add_IdWithMarkdownPunctuation_IsRefused` — `|`, `]`, `(`, `)` break the Slice cell's
   link even though S21 keeps the row well-formed.
3. `SlicePath_IdEscapingTheSlicesDirectory_IsRefused` — the belt-and-braces check, so a
   hand-edited index cannot do it either.
4. `Migrate_TreeWithATraversingId_RefusesToWrite`.
5. `Verify_StoredIdBreakingTheRule_IsReported`.

sections.heading: Implement
sections.body:
One rule, shared: an id is a run of characters that is safe both as a filename and inside
a markdown link — letters, digits, `-`, `_`, `.` but not `..`, and nothing else. Reject at
`ids.allocate` (covering `add --id`), in the migrator when adopting ids, and assert in
`store.slice_path` that the resolved path is still inside the slices directory, so a
hand-edited `index.json` cannot reach past it either.

Resolve-and-compare is the check that actually holds: string matching on `..` misses
symlinks and absolute paths.

Existing bad ids cannot be renamed — ids are never reused and a rename would break every
citation — so `verify` reports them and the owner decides.

**Not in this slice:** a general policy for unicode in ids. The rule above is ASCII, which
is what the default scheme produces; widening it is a separate decision.

sections.heading: Check
sections.body: Every id in the Why section is refused, and `migrate` refuses the tree.
